sm: Albert Mohler opens the Friday, November sixth briefing by discussing the Washington Post's first ever divorce week, a series of stories on the good, bad, ugly, sad, happy and strange sides of ending a marriage. He quotes an editorial writer who says his go-to line for divorcing friends is congratulations and condolences, and that divorce is always on some level for the best. Mohler says this treats divorce as a rite of passage, when it is the ending of a covenant meant to last until death. He also notes a Wall Street Journal front-page story about divorce lawyers whose clients bring them legal advice from artificial intelligence. He closes the segment with novelist Pat Conroy's line that divorce is the death of a small civilization, which he says matches the biblical creation order.

Mohler says that today divorce is often seen as liberation and personal autonomy rather than a moral scandal, and that Christians should at least think about marriage through the biblical creation order. He then turns to listener questions. A twelve-year-old boy asks where the souls of Lazarus and Jairus's daughter went before Jesus raised them. Mohler explains the intermediate state, in which believers' souls are with Christ before the resurrection of the body, and says he believes the two were safe under Christ's lordship and not yet glorified. He then starts on a question from Melissa in Texas about God's sovereignty and elections after a conservative loss, beginning with the example of choosing a ketchup at the supermarket.

Mohler continues with the point that people really choose among things like ice cream flavors, as his colleague Bruce Ware puts it, while all of it sits within God's sovereign will, an idea he ties to the Latin word concursus. He says voting matters more than ice cream, and Christians should vote for the platform closest to their convictions, rest in God's sovereignty, and still take up their responsibilities. Answering another listener who wanted him to stress sovereignty after the election, he says he is confident God is on his throne, and that he does believe this week's outcome is in some sense God's judgment on the country. A student in Cambridge, England, then asks where Reformed Christians should draw the line on images of Christ. Mohler says he is Puritan-leaning and wary, because we have revealed words about Christ and not revealed pictures, though he notes that images have long been used to teach the unlettered, as in medieval stained glass.

Mohler says he is uncomfortable with artistic depictions of Christ and owns none, though he loves art and has paintings of Luther, Calvin and Jonathan Edwards, plus a framed portion of a famous painting showing the Apostle John pointing to Jesus. He explains that Reformed churches differ on this, noting the Lutheran view that what is not forbidden is allowed, against Calvin's view that what is not commanded should not be done. He says the Reformed majority is suspicious of depicting the Father, Son or Spirit, but he is not on a crusade and would not tear a page from a children's Bible, though children should be told we do not know what Jesus looked like. He rejects any idea of revelation through images, as in Eastern Orthodoxy and much of Catholicism, and says he worries less about this with children than with adults. He then closes with his usual website information and says he will be back Monday.
